key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum default reduced flat minimum-payment enrollment by 23% at 6 months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, and increased missed payments among liquidity-constrained cardholders.
methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with 6-month follow-up; behavioral analysis of autopay enrollment and payment amounts.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether nudging users into a different default payment behavior actually changes financial outcomes in a self-directed consumer financial product, showing the enrollment/behavior gap and harm to a subgroup that our Entry decision must weigh.
limitations: credit card debt repayment rather than savings enrollment
outcome is autopay minimum payment behavior, not a round-up feature
relevance_reason: Closest real consumer-financial field experiment testing whether a default/nudge in a self-directed banking product changes both enrollment and actual financial amounts, revealing harm to a subgroup.

key_finding: A narrative overview of DC retirement plan design summarizing known effects of automatic enrollment, default investments, and framing on participation and engagement, without new estimates.
methodology: Narrative literature overview; abstract-only synthesis, no primary data.
why_it_matters: Provides a broad map of the employer-retirement default literature but offers no new effect sizes or consumer-setting evidence, so it does not move either the Entry or Level decision beyond what more targeted papers already show.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement setting, not consumer self-directed product
narrative rather than systematic review
no quantitative effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Background context on the employer-retirement default literature the brief flags as adjacent but not directly transferable.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment in retirement plans raises short-term participation but induces long-term passivity (low contribution rates, account churn), recommending auto-escalation and reminders to offset this.
methodology: Narrative policy commentary; abstract-only, no original empirical data.
why_it_matters: Echoes the support team's disengagement concern in a retirement context, but as unsupported commentary it adds little beyond stronger empirical papers already in the set.
limitations: employer retirement plan setting
no empirical data or effect sizes
very low citation count, appears to be a minor commentary piece
relevance_reason: Restates the passive-enrollment concern central to the brief's trade-off, but with no new evidence.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for 'downstream' default effects on consumer behavior, identifying time-course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators of whether default effects persist or fade.
methodology: Conceptual review and framework synthesis of the consumer-default literature; abstract-only detail on individual studies.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to predict and measure whether the round-up default's enrollment effect will persist or decay, flagging exactly the moderators our post-launch measurement plan should track.
limitations: theoretical/synthesis paper, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: The most recent synthesis specifically about downstream (persistence, disengagement) effects of defaults in consumer behavior, giving a measurement framework rather than a single effect size.

key_finding: Using natural experiments in Medicare Part D, default enrollment has large, persistent effects on drug plan enrollment, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even when it induces large losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative dataset of Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that default-driven passivity can be robust even against personal financial cost, raising the stakes of choosing opt-out for a product where passive enrollment could similarly stick regardless of fit.
limitations: health insurance / government program setting, not consumer financial self-directed product
no discussion of amount saved or preset-level anchoring
relevance_reason: Rigorous evidence on how insensitive default-driven passivity can be, relevant by analogy but off-domain so capped.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and auto-escalation defaults on 401(k) savings: steady-state saving rates rise by only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalation defaults are followed at the first escalation date.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, withdrawal upon separation, and auto-escalation opt-out over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified rebuttal of the premise that defaults reliably and durably lift savings, directly supporting the support team's 'vanity metric' concern once turnover, withdrawal, and later opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: retirement 401(k) plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives aggregate effect sizes but not distributional detail
relevance_reason: The strongest available quantified contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise, precisely the counter-evidence the brief asks for.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into the public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out, with the default effect strongest when incentives are high and enrollment-status knowledge is low.
methodology: Quasi-experimental analysis of a nationwide policy rollout, linking administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Shows the size of a default effect is highly conditional on incentive strength and consumer knowledge, informing how much enrolment lift to expect and for whom.
limitations: public pension system, not a consumer fintech product
abstract gives no data on amount saved or persistence beyond the initial opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Recent large-scale quasi-experimental evidence on default-effect heterogeneity by incentive and knowledge, relevant to who is helped vs hurt, though in a pension rather than consumer setting.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains replicate at 12 months but attenuate substantially by 36 months, though it durably reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250, smaller than prior estimates.
methodology: Data from over 100 US retirement plans and a representative UK panel; life-cycle consumption-savings structural model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's central question of whether the default effect persists at 6-12 months and beyond, showing decay over the medium run and setting realistic expectations for post-launch enrollment metrics.
limitations: retirement savings plans, not liquid consumer savings
structural model relies on modeling assumptions to interpret attenuation
relevance_reason: The most rigorous and recent large-sample estimate of exactly how default effects on enrollment/contribution attenuate over time, the strongest available evidence on the persistence question.

key_finding: A representative five-country European experiment (n=4207) finds defaults produce medium-to-large effects on financial risk-taking, but also lower ratings of advisor honesty and advice quality when a default is used or refused, especially a one-size-fits-all default.
methodology: Three experiments including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment on default framing in investment decisions.
why_it_matters: Direct EU evidence linking default strength to perceived manipulativeness/trust cost, especially when applied uniformly, exactly the reputational risk the brief flags for opt-out enrollment.
limitations: wealth-management advice context with human advisor mediation, not a fully self-directed app
no data on persistence or amount saved over time
relevance_reason: The clearest EU evidence connecting default strength to perceived manipulativeness/trust cost, directly informing whether opt-out enrollment risks a dark-pattern perception.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation to over 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still at the default rate and fund after three years, offsetting wealth-accumulation gains from higher participation.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking savings behavior and asset allocation over multiple years under automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset contribution level anchors most enrollees for years, warning that whichever round-up multiplier we preselect will likely become the durable norm for most users, shaping which multiplier to choose.
limitations: 401(k) employer-plan setting, not a consumer app
no publication year given; an older foundational study
relevance_reason: The classic empirical demonstration of anchoring on a preset contribution level, the specific mechanism the brief's Level decision turns on.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost, and adding a lower preset option (15%) to the existing menu could capture 69% of the achievable consumer-welfare gain at only a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey to identify true preferences separate from default influence.
why_it_matters: Provides a directly transferable method for testing whether our 1x/2x/5x preset menu anchors users away from their true preferred round-up level, and shows adding one more menu option can recover most welfare loss cheaply, a concrete lever for the Level decision.
limitations: tipping decisions rather than savings enrollment
single-decision snapshot, not longitudinal savings behavior
relevance_reason: A rigorous structural-model method for decomposing why users stick with a preset option, directly transferable to testing whether our multiplier menu anchors choices away from true preference.

key_finding: In an opt-in short-term, withdrawable payroll savings program at five UK firms, no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account, but among activators, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Administrative panel data from an opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings program across five UK firms, tracked over 12 months.
why_it_matters: The closest available evidence on a liquid, withdrawable consumer savings product under opt-in: enrollment is very low but persistence among enrollees is very high, exactly the opt-in trade-off (low reach, good depth) the Entry decision needs to weigh against opt-out.
limitations: employer-payroll intermediary rather than a self-directed banking app
does not report amount saved, only balance presence and contribution occurrence
relevance_reason: The nearest real-world analog to a liquid, withdrawable round-up-style savings product studied under opt-in, directly informing the enrollment-vs-persistence trade-off for the Entry decision.

key_finding: Derives a general characterization of optimal default options via asymptotic analysis, showing that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions for externalities and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical economic model with asymptotic/limiting-case analysis, validated through numerical simulations; no empirical data.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative theoretical benchmark for when a strong opt-out-style default is welfare-justified versus risky given designer-user disagreement, useful as a conceptual check but purely theoretical.
limitations: fully theoretical with no empirical application or specific setting
no data on consumer financial products or enrollment
relevance_reason: General normative theory for choosing default strength that could frame the Entry decision's welfare trade-off, though abstract and unvalidated in this setting.

key_finding: Maps EU law on dark patterns and develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations that distinguishes acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable manipulation.
methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis of EU consumer-protection law; normative taxonomy construction. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's reputational-risk question — when a pre-selected default (e.g., opt-out enrolment, pre-set multiplier) crosses from helpful into a regulable EU dark pattern — and should shape how entry and level defaults are framed and disclosed.
limitations: legal/normative, not empirical: gives no enrolment or persistence effect sizes
framework, not a tested measurement of user perception
relevance_reason: Provides the EU-specific legal/normative framework for assessing whether the chosen default design is a manipulative dark pattern, which is exactly the reputational constraint the brief names.

key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out at 12 months (vs. ~50% at lower defaults in prior literature), and non-opters' contributions clustered at the suboptimal 12% default rather than at levels their income would predict.
methodology: Field data from an employer retirement plan with a high (12%) default contribution rate; literature review comparison. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: The strongest available evidence that a preset level anchors people at a suboptimal rate and that default persistence at 12 months is substantial — directly bears on the round-up multiplier anchoring question, but only by analogy since it is an employer-mediated pension default.
limitations: employer-mediated retirement plan, not a consumer self-directed liquid savings product
no data on later withdrawal/disengagement beyond contribution rate persistence
relevance_reason: Closest available quantified evidence on default persistence and anchoring at a preset contribution level, though in the excluded employer-pension setting.

key_finding: Abstract is not usable (contains only the word 'Trant'); no extractable finding on payroll savings automation from four UK experiments.
methodology: abstract-only; title indicates UK payroll savings automation experiments but no methodological detail is available.
why_it_matters: Title suggests direct relevance (automated short-term savings, UK, multiple experiments) but the abstract gives nothing to act on, so it cannot currently inform any decision.
limitations: abstract essentially empty, no data or effect sizes retrievable
payroll savings is employer-mediated, not consumer app self-directed
relevance_reason: Topically close to round-up savings automation but abstract provides no usable evidence.

key_finding: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks show automatic enrolment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide annually, though alerts capture less than half of consumers' potential savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run with UK retail banks on automatic enrolment into alert features.
why_it_matters: The closest available evidence: a UK bank automatically enrolling retail customers into a consumer financial feature at scale, with quantified behavioural and monetary effects — this is the direct precedent for what auto-enrolling users into round-up savings could plausibly achieve and where its limits lie.
limitations: measures overdraft-alert behaviour, not a savings/round-up product specifically
no explicit 6-12 month disengagement or withdrawal analysis reported in the abstract
relevance_reason: Nearest real-world analogue: UK consumer bank auto-enrolment into a financial-behaviour feature with quantified effect sizes at scale.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrolment increases savings but each additional month raises average unsecured debt by about £7 and mortgage balances by £118 over 41 months, partially offsetting the savings gain, while also modestly improving credit scores and defaults.
methodology: Natural experiment from randomized roll-out of UK automatic-enrolment pensions across ~160,000 small employers, 41-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Cautions that headline enrolment/savings gains from a default can be partly illusory once broader financial behaviour (debt) is accounted for — relevant to the support team's worry that passively-enrolled savers may be worse off net, even though the setting is pensions not liquid round-up savings.
limitations: employer-mediated pension automatic enrolment, not a consumer self-directed liquid savings app
offset effect measured in debt, not directly in round-up savings withdrawal/disengagement
relevance_reason: Provides distributional/welfare evidence that default-driven enrolment can produce offsetting harms, informing the brief's concern about who is helped versus hurt.

key_finding: Removing auto-enrolment and adding a minor enrolment 'ordeal' step reduced health insurance enrolment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying policy change (removal of auto-enrolment) in a public health-insurance program, with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Shows that adding friction to enrolment (analogous to opt-in or active choice relative to opt-out) can produce large, distributionally uneven drops in participation — relevant caution for how much enrolment loss active choice or opt-in might cost, and who bears it.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a consumer savings/fintech product
adverse-selection dynamics specific to insurance markets may not transfer to savings enrolment
relevance_reason: Quantifies how much enrolment-design friction can cost and who it disproportionately excludes, informing the active-choice-versus-default trade-off by analogy.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation default boxes on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not compensate by adjusting amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting different rollout timing of default checkboxes across 2020 U.S. campaign websites.
why_it_matters: A genuine consumer, self-directed, digital-transaction default (not employer-mediated) showing both a large enrolment/behaviour effect and a refund/complaint signature that mirrors the support team's worry about passively-enrolled users disengaging or complaining.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product, so amounts and stakes differ
no measurement of outcomes beyond the immediate donation/refund window (no 6-12 month follow-up)
relevance_reason: Closest evidence of a consumer digital default producing both a strong enrolment effect and a dark-pattern-like complaint/refund cost, directly bearing on the trade-off the brief is deciding.

key_finding: Lab experiments confirm that a default option raises the reservation utility for search (a reference effect) and that people with higher reservation utility self-select into active search and find better options.
methodology: Theoretical search model with reference-dependent utility tested via laboratory experiments.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanism (reference-dependent search) for why defaults change behaviour, but it is abstract search theory rather than evidence on enrolment, persistence, or anchoring in a financial product.
limitations: laboratory search task, not a financial enrolment or savings-level decision
no consumer financial product setting
relevance_reason: Background theoretical mechanism for default effects on choice; too abstract to change enrolment or level design directly.

key_finding: After the EU Digital Markets Act mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting from 15 months after rollout onward.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the EU DMA choice-screen mandate rollout across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether an EU-mandated active-choice screen can meaningfully shift behaviour away from an entrenched default, with effects sustained over a year — the closest available quantified evidence on whether active choice captures most of a default's benefit, in the exact EU regulatory context the brief operates in.
limitations: studies default browser choice, not a financial savings enrolment decision
platform-specific rollout mechanics (new vs. existing devices) complicate direct transfer of magnitude
relevance_reason: Provides the strongest quantified, persistent evidence comparing an EU-mandated active-choice mechanism against an entrenched default, directly informing the active-choice design option.

key_finding: In a 410-participant usability study, generalizable active-choice opt-out interface designs reduced disruption (98% not disrupted for the best scheme, a 40-point improvement) at a slight cost to opt-out utility, while 83% of participants understood the mechanism and made intentional choices.
methodology: Design and usability study of nine active-choice (no-default) interface schemes implemented in a browser extension, tested with 410 participants.
why_it_matters: Offers concrete UI patterns for making a forced active-choice step feel less disruptive without silently defaulting users, directly relevant to designing the onboarding screen if active choice is chosen — but the setting is privacy opt-out, not financial enrolment.
limitations: privacy opt-out context (CCPA/GPC), not a financial product
effects measured on disruption/comprehension, not enrolment or savings outcomes
relevance_reason: Provides transferable active-choice interface design principles for reducing onboarding friction, relevant to the active-choice design option though not in a financial setting.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-up uptake, but only increased actual effortful completion (exam passing) for students who were already responsive to university communication; non-responsive students showed increased sign-up with no effect on the effortful target outcome.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up procedure to opt-out in two study programs, tracking sign-up, participation, and passing.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the exact mechanism the support team fears: a default can raise nominal enrolment without changing effortful downstream behaviour, and the split is driven by pre-existing responsiveness — a template for how to test whether round-up enrolment translates into actual saving.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial or digital consumer product
'responsiveness' proxy may not map onto financial engagement predictors
relevance_reason: Provides a close mechanistic analogy for the brief's central worry — that opt-out raises enrolment without changing effortful engagement — with heterogeneity by responsiveness.

key_finding: Making target-date funds the default investment option shifted the age-dependence of stock market exposure but contribution rates changed little following the default change.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. retirement investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act's default rule change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default changing which asset option people passively hold without moving contribution levels, a weak secondary signal that default effects on 'level' choices can be uneven — but the setting and lever (asset allocation default) are distant from the round-up multiplier decision.
limitations: employer retirement plan asset-allocation default, not a contribution-level or enrolment decision
no consumer/self-directed liquid savings context
relevance_reason: Marginally relevant as evidence that a preset default did not move contribution levels, a weak counterpoint on anchoring, but in an excluded pension setting.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, default-option and positive-narrative nudges significantly reduced willingness to contribute and the proportion of income saved, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with effects varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension saving decisions.
why_it_matters: The clearest available contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise the brief explicitly asked us to test against, plus heterogeneity by income/education/gender that speaks directly to who a default might harm.
limitations: small online-survey sample (n=220) measuring stated willingness rather than real enrolment behaviour
voluntary pension saving in China, a different cultural/regulatory context than an EU consumer banking app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving and provides the distributional heterogeneity evidence the brief asked for.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people rated financial nudges neutral-to-positive overall, preferred System 2 (reflective) interventions and savings-framed messaging over spending-framed ones, and transparency had no significant effect on approval.
methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment across 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios, representative Australian sample (n=2,100).
why_it_matters: Directly measures when a financial nudge or default is perceived as manipulative versus helpful, which is exactly the dark-pattern reputational-risk question the brief raises for an EU opt-out design, and suggests savings-framed, reflective (System 2) messaging is preferred.
limitations: hypothetical scenarios rather than a live banking product
measures stated approval, not actual enrolment or saving behavior
Australian sample, not EU regulatory context
relevance_reason: Provides the most direct evidence in this batch on perceived manipulativeness/approval of financial nudges, bearing on the manipulation-risk criterion.

key_finding: Offering CCT recipients a bank-account delivery option instead of cash produced no significant average effect on savings or downstream trust/assets, but increased balances for those who previously had nonpositive balances.
methodology: Randomized offering of delivery channel to conditional-cash-transfer beneficiaries; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Suggests account-based delivery mainly helps those with no prior savings, a mild distributional data point, but says nothing about enrolment-design levers (opt-in/opt-out/active choice) for a self-directed app.
limitations: low-income CCT population in a developing-country welfare program, not an EU banking app user base
not about opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment design
relevance_reason: Tangential evidence on account-based delivery and heterogeneous savings response among low-balance individuals.

key_finding: Abstract is fragmentary; it only states that contribution amounts and program benefits on liquid emergency-savings funds do not differ between the compared program cases.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to compare automatic-IRA program variants including an emergency-savings feature.
why_it_matters: Nominally touches automatic enrolment combined with liquid savings, close to our round-up concept, but the abstract offers no usable statistics or design comparison.
limitations: abstract is garbled/incomplete, no extractable findings
auto-IRA is a state/employer-facilitated payroll vehicle, not a self-directed banking app
relevance_reason: Title suggests relevance to automatic enrolment with liquid savings, but content is unusable.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and many employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation even though almost none had chosen that combination voluntarily.
methodology: Before/after natural-experiment analysis of administrative 401(k) data from one large U.S. corporation.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration of default power and anchoring in retirement saving; useful background but superseded here by Choi et al. and Chetty et al., which give more direct persistence and amount-saved evidence.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) with employer as trusted intermediary, unlike a self-directed banking app
single-firm study, 2001 data
no data on 6-12 month withdrawal or amount actually saved beyond the default rate
relevance_reason: Foundational default/anchoring result the later literature (including this batch's stronger papers) builds on and argues with.

key_finding: No abstract available; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviors under automatic versus voluntary enrollment in a defined-contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only; no abstract text provided.
why_it_matters: Could in principle add another data point on auto- vs. voluntary-enrollment savings outcomes, but with no abstract there is nothing concrete to weigh against the decision.
limitations: no abstract available to assess methodology or findings
employer-sponsored defined-contribution plan context
relevance_reason: Title-only relevance to auto- vs. voluntary-enrolment comparison; no usable content.

key_finding: Across three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension reform, limited institutional trust and non-Estonian nationality were both associated with lower regular pension saving and higher likelihood of early withdrawal.
methodology: Observational analysis of three national representative surveys surrounding a mandatory-pension-freedom reform.
why_it_matters: Shows the same low-trust, minority-status users who under-save are also the ones most likely to withdraw early, a distributional warning directly relevant to which users might disengage or withdraw quickly after passive enrolment in the round-up feature.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme in Estonia, not a self-directed liquid digital savings product
correlational survey data, not causal
withdrawal here is a one-off policy-driven choice, not gradual app disengagement
relevance_reason: Distributional evidence on who is more likely to under-save and withdraw early, informing the brief's who-is-helped/who-is-hurt concern.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment vaccination policy reduced their stated intention to comply and decreased approval of the policy, contrary to expectations.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries testing reflection on a hypothetical default-enrollment health policy.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that making a default salient can backfire, reducing both compliance intentions and approval, a caution against assuming an opt-out design is perceived as neutral once users notice they were auto-enrolled.
limitations: public-health/vaccination domain, not a financial product
measures stated intentions in a hypothetical scenario, not actual behavior
no financial enrolment or amount-saved outcome
relevance_reason: Rare evidence that highlighting a default can trigger backlash rather than acceptance, bearing on the manipulation/dark-pattern risk question despite the health-policy setting.

key_finding: Using 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study data, automatic enrollment and employer-matching contributions were associated with a higher likelihood of retirement-plan participation among Millennials.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the well-established auto-enrolment participation lift in an employer plan; adds little new beyond stronger foundational studies already in the evidence set.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan with employer as trusted intermediary
cross-sectional, not causal
no data on withdrawal, amount saved, or active-choice comparison
relevance_reason: Confirmatory employer-plan evidence on the auto-enrolment participation lift, largely redundant with stronger studies.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations from Denmark, automatic employer contributions increased total wealth accumulation substantially, while subsidies requiring active choice raised saving by only about 1 cent per $1 of government cost, because roughly 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily influenced by automatic contributions.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel analysis of the Danish population comparing active-choice tax subsidies to passive/automatic retirement contributions.
why_it_matters: The largest-scale, most rigorous evidence that defaults change real wealth accumulation for most people rather than just nominal enrolment, directly bearing on the support team's 'vanity enrolment' objection, even though the employer/government contribution mechanism differs from a self-directed app default.
limitations: government/employer-administered retirement accounts, not a self-directed consumer banking app
tests contribution-rate responses to subsidies, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment mechanics directly
Danish tax/administrative context, not EU consumer fintech
relevance_reason: Strongest available large-scale evidence on whether default-driven contributions change real savings amounts versus nominal enrolment via active choice, the core amount-vs-enrolment question the brief asks.

key_finding: An 'enhanced active choice' design — forced choice that highlights losses from the non-preferred option — is proposed and tested across several studies, including two field experiments, as an effective complement or alternative to opt-out defaults for motivating behavior change.
methodology: Literature review plus two field experiments testing active choice and a novel enhanced-active-choice design.
why_it_matters: Directly informs the entry-mode decision: whether active/forced choice, especially an enhanced version nudging toward one answer, can capture much of an opt-out default's enrolment benefit without the same manipulation/ethics exposure.
limitations: original studies are in medication adherence and general savings contexts, not a mobile banking round-up feature
abstract does not report quantitative enrolment or persistence effect sizes
relevance_reason: The closest available prior work proposing and testing active choice as a design alternative to opt-out defaults, directly the third entry-mode option under decision.

key_finding: A broad review chapter summarizing behavioral regularities in household consumption, saving, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and cataloguing intervention types including choice architecture, product design and default-based interventions.
methodology: Narrative literature review / NBER book chapter on behavioral household finance; abstract-only detail on specific effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Offers useful background synthesis of choice-architecture interventions across consumer financial behaviors, but is too broad and unfocused on enrolment-default effect sizes to move either the entry-mode or level-design decision on its own.
limitations: broad overview, not focused specifically on enrolment defaults or their effect sizes
abstract gives no quantitative synthesis of default effects
relevance_reason: General reference review on behavioral household finance and choice architecture, useful context rather than decision-specific evidence.

key_finding: Across three large firms, automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants stuck with the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and a conservative default fund, and even after three years half remained at the default — so the participation gain and the low default savings rate roughly offset in net asset accumulation, though the lower tail of the distribution still benefited.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms before and after automatic-enrollment adoption.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative evidence that a pre-set contribution level anchors most users for years, directly bearing on whether our round-up multiplier default (1x/2x/5x) will anchor users at whatever level we pre-select, and a caution that a higher nominal enrolment rate can be offset by a low chosen level.
limitations: employer 401(k) with an employer-selected default, not a consumer app
three-firm sample from around 2001
does not examine liquid-savings withdrawal or disengagement
relevance_reason: The strongest available longitudinal evidence that a pre-set contribution level anchors participant choices for years, directly informing the round-up multiplier default-level decision.

key_finding: In a randomized field experiment, default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% matching incentive), driven largely by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of choosing, and also made people more likely to actively choose to save even after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among employees in Afghanistan varying default savings-account enrollment, with follow-up interventions to test mechanism explanations.
why_it_matters: Disentangles why defaults work — present bias and decision cost rather than trust in an employer intermediary — evidence that the default mechanism should still operate in a self-directed consumer app lacking an employer as trusted intermediary.
limitations: salary-linked account among employees in a low-income-country context, not an EU banking app
does not report amounts saved or 6-12 month withdrawal specifically
no comparison to an active-choice enrolment condition
relevance_reason: Clearest available mechanism evidence for why default effects occur, addressing the exact employer-trust-mechanism gap the brief flags between the pension literature and our consumer app setting.

key_finding: Payment reminders in a Brazilian financial-management app cut credit card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who already had overdraft history seeing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a consumer financial management platform in Brazil, measuring fee outcomes across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's core worry that a nudge helping most users on average can actively harm a vulnerable subgroup, arguing for heterogeneity-aware evaluation before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit card/overdraft fee context rather than a savings round-up product
no data on persistence beyond the experiment window
relevance_reason: Strongest available consumer-fintech RCT evidence that nudge-style interventions can produce distributional harm, speaking to C5 even though it doesn't address entry mechanism or anchoring.
